header.tag_why: The rep blames price, but the CFO judged the switch on a rate-only one-pager where the only thing from us was our quote. No Fernbrook figure was ever put on the one-in-twelve failing orders, even though Farah offered to build one and Lucy asked for a business case, so he saw "the same thing" at a higher price.

evidence.excerpt: Their ecommerce director, Lucy, came inbound.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: She said about one in twelve online orders was failing at the payment step, and it was worse on the big baskets.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Her number. Off their own dashboard.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: she couldn't get a straight answer from the processor on why.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: This deal started with a quantified, self-measured problem: failing orders, worst on high-value items, plus an incumbent that couldn't explain why. That is exactly the raw material for a business case. The trigger was a revenue-loss problem, but the deal ended as a rate comparison, so we let the original pain fall out of the final decision.
trigger.messaging: Open these deals on the customer's own failure rate and what it costs on big-ticket orders, not on M1's global-growth line, and carry that number through to the final decision document.

evidence.excerpt: The CFO, Martin. Lucy was the champion, she wanted it, IT was fine with it. Martin said no.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Lucy told me. I never met him.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Lucy said he doesn't take vendor meetings and she'd carry it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Martin and the controller. I wasn't in the room. Lucy presented it.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: The decider was a CFO we never reached. Everything we know about his reasoning reaches us third-hand. Accepting 'she'd carry it' was reasonable only if we armed Lucy to carry it, and we sent her into the room with a deck and a price.
decider.messaging: When we can't reach the CFO, our champion needs a finance-ready, one-page case built on their own numbers, written for someone who never saw the demo.

evidence.excerpt: They were on Fiserv through their bank, had been forever.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: when the bank heard, they came back and sharpened the rate.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Up to then Lucy was asking about declines. Why big orders fail, what we'd do about it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: After the bank came back, every email was the rate.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: The bank's rate cut didn't just lower its price. It moved the whole evaluation from declines, where we were winning, to rate, where the incumbent wins by default. We followed it there instead of pulling it back. Nothing in the transcript suggests the bank addressed the failing orders it had never explained.
competitor.messaging: When an incumbent bank counters on rate, reframe on cost per completed order: the unexplained declines plus the costs the rep says sit off the statement line (gateway fee, chargeback handling). Never answer a rate email with a rate.

evidence.excerpt: Lucy was nodding the whole way.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Lucy loved the checkout. And the decline piece.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Silence, honestly, nothing bombed. It was a good cycle. We lost on price.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: We showed the uplift slide. The average improvement in acceptance.
evidence.label: fact

message.insight: What landed was Farah's specific explanation of why big-ticket orders get knocked back. That is diagnosis, not a generic claim. The rep says nothing got silence, but the generic average-uplift message (M4) evidently never travelled to the CFO, who called it "the same thing". The silence happened in the room we weren't in.
message.messaging: Replace M4's average-uplift claim with a diagnosis of the prospect's own declines and what those failed orders are worth, because the specific explanation is what got a reaction.

evidence.excerpt: Right before that she'd been telling me it was a formality.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: he's not going to pay more for the same thing.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: The controller did a one-pager for Martin. Our rate, their rate, side by side.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Our quote.
evidence.label: fact

decided.insight: The deal was decided by a document the customer's controller wrote. It compared per-transaction rates only, and our sole contribution was the quote. The champion's 'formality' read shows that neither she nor we saw that the decision would be framed as a rate check. The rep's own hedge, that a matched rate would still read 'same rate, so why move', undercuts his conclusion that price alone killed it.
decided.messaging: Never let a rate-only comparison be the decision document; give the champion our own one-pager that puts the cost of failed orders next to the rate.

evidence.excerpt: Lucy asked once if we had something she could hand Martin. Like a one-page business case.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I sent her the deck and the pricing proposal.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Farah offered to run their declines. She wanted a three-month export so she could show what the failed orders were worth.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: it was the last two weeks of the quarter, and I didn't want to slow things down.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: This was not a product gap. It was a proof gap we chose not to close: the customer asked for a business case, our SE offered the analysis to build it, and the rep skipped it to protect quarter-end timing. Customer stories and an average uplift were offered as the business case. A CFO reads those as marketing, not as Fernbrook's numbers.
gaps.messaging: Make the decline-export value analysis a standard step before pricing goes to finance, and treat M6/M8 proof as backup, never as the business case.

evidence.excerpt: orders dying at the last step.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: the big baskets.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Why would I pay more for the same thing.
evidence.label: quote

language.insight: Lucy speaks in lost orders and wasted effort on big baskets. We spoke in authorization rates and acceptance uplift, and the CFO heard "the same thing". The rep gives two different wordings of Martin's line (T16 vs T24), so it should be treated as the gist rather than verbatim.
language.messaging: Use the customer's own phrasing, such as orders dying at the last step and the big baskets, in place of 'authorization rates' in M4, and translate it into lost revenue for finance.

gaps.question: What did Martin have in front of him about what one in twelve failing orders was costing?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy: did the failed-order problem or its cost come up in the meeting with Martin, and what did he say about it?

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Farah and Sam: what did Lucy not react to or not repeat back, and did the uplift slide ever get a question from her?

gaps.question: If we had matched the price, would we have won?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy: if our rate had equalled the bank's, would Martin have approved, given the IT lead's concern about moving before spring?

gaps.question: What exactly did Martin say, and was there any other reason?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy: what were Martin's exact words, and did he raise anything besides the rate, such as timing or switching risk?

gaps.question: How big was the gap between our quote and the bank's sharpened rate?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Sam (and the deal desk): what were the two per-transaction numbers on the controller's one-pager?

gaps.question: Are the gateway fee and dedicated chargeback person real, and what do they cost?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy: what does Fernbrook pay in gateway fees and chargeback handling today?

gaps.question: Has the bank's offer done anything about the failing orders?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy in a check-in: is the one-in-twelve failure rate still where it was since they stayed?

close.rep_takeaway: When the champion asks for something to hand the decider, treat that as the deal, not a side request. Farah's three-month decline analysis was the one thing that could have turned 'the same thing' into a number Martin had to weigh, and quarter-end pressure is exactly when skipping it costs the most. If we can't get in the room, our proof has to: nothing walks in for us unless we write it.
